meta.title: Struck-By Hazards in Construction Environments
meta.description: Learn to recognize fall hazards and falling object hazards, apply OSHA 1910.28 protection requirements, and use guardrails, covers, personal fall protection, and falling object controls correctly.
meta.oshaStandard: 29 CFR 1910.28 — Duty to Have Fall Protection and Falling Object Protection

lessons.fall-protection-overview:
**Why Fall Protection Matters**

Falls and falling objects can occur during routine tasks on familiar surfaces — not just during high-risk operations. A loading dock, mezzanine, stairway, roof, or ladder can become dangerous when employees work near an edge, opening, hole, or unprotected lower level. OSHA 1910.28 establishes the employer's duty to protect employees from fall hazards and falling object hazards on walking-working surfaces. It applies to a wide range of situations including elevated platforms, holes, openings, hoist areas, dockboards, runways, fixed ladders, stairs, roofs, pits, and scaffolds. Temporary tasks do not exempt employers or employees from fall protection requirements. Proactive hazard recognition and early reporting are the most effective prevention strategies.

• Falls can happen during routine tasks on familiar surfaces, not only during high-risk work.
• OSHA 1910.28 places a clear duty on employers to protect employees from fall and falling object hazards.
• Temporary tasks do not remove the requirement for fall protection.
• Fall hazards covered include holes, skylights, hoist areas, roofs, fixed ladders, and stairways.
lessons.unprotected-edges-surfaces:
**Unprotected Sides, Edges, and Walking-Working Surfaces**

The general fall protection trigger under OSHA 1910.28 is 4 feet above a lower level for unprotected sides, edges, and walking-working surfaces in general industry. When employees are exposed at this height or greater, employers must provide protection using a guardrail system, safety net system, personal fall arrest system, travel restraint system, or positioning system. No single method is required — any acceptable system that meets OSHA criteria may be used. Acceptable methods are defined in OSHA 1910.29 (fall protection and falling object protection criteria) and OSHA 1910.140 (personal fall protection systems). Common exposures include mezzanines, raised storage platforms, elevated walkways, and open-sided work platforms.

• The general fall protection trigger is 4 feet above a lower level for most walking-working surfaces.
• Acceptable protection includes guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall protection systems.
• No single method is mandated — any compliant system meeting OSHA criteria may be used.
• OSHA 1910.29 and 1910.140 provide criteria for compliant fall protection systems.
lessons.holes-openings-hatchways:
**Holes, Openings, Hatchways, and Ladderway Floor Holes**

Employees must be protected from falling through floor holes, skylights, stairway holes, hatchways, chute holes, and ladderway openings. When a hole is 4 feet or more above a lower level, cover or guarding is required to prevent falls. Even holes less than 4 feet above a lower level must be protected to prevent tripping or stepping through. Ladderway floor holes require guardrail systems and toeboards on exposed sides, with a self-closing gate or offset at the entrance. An uncovered hole must be reported immediately, kept clear of personnel, and covered or guarded by authorized personnel before work resumes in the area. Temporary coverings must be secured to prevent displacement.

• Holes 4 feet or more above a lower level must be covered or guarded to prevent falls.
• Holes less than 4 feet above must be protected to prevent tripping or stepping through.
• Ladderway floor holes require guardrail systems, toeboards, and a self-closing gate or offset.
• An uncovered hole must be reported and protected before employees continue working near it.
lessons.hoist-areas-dockboards:
**Hoist Areas, Dockboards, Runways, and Dangerous Equipment**

Hoist areas where employees could fall 4 feet or more generally require guardrails, personal fall arrest systems, or travel restraint systems. When guardrail chains or gates are removed and an employee must lean through or over the opening — such as to guide a load — a personal fall arrest system is specifically required. Dockboards, runways, and narrow walkways have requirements based on height and use. Employees near dangerous equipment must be protected from falls even when below the 4-foot threshold, because contact with the equipment itself creates a hazard. Employers must plan load-handling operations to maintain protection during active hoisting.

• Hoist areas require guardrails, personal fall arrest, or travel restraint when exposure is 4 feet or more.
• When a guardrail is removed for hoisting and a worker leans over the opening, a personal fall arrest system is required.
• Employees near dangerous equipment must be protected even below 4 feet if contact would be hazardous.
• Protection must be maintained throughout hoisting operations, not just before and after.
lessons.ladders-stairs-scaffolds:
**Fixed Ladders, Stairs, Scaffolds, and Rope Descent Systems**

Fixed ladders extending more than 24 feet above a lower level have specific fall protection requirements under OSHA 1910.28. New fixed ladders installed on or after November 19, 2018 must be equipped with a personal fall arrest system or ladder safety system. OSHA established a final compliance deadline of November 18, 2036 for all fixed ladders in this category to be equipped with one of these systems. Stairways with four or more risers or rising more than 30 inches generally require stair rail systems or handrails. Scaffolds and rope descent systems also have specific fall protection requirements under OSHA 1910.28 and their respective standards.

• Fixed ladders over 24 feet above a lower level require fall protection under OSHA 1910.28.
• New fixed ladders installed on or after November 19, 2018 must have a personal fall arrest or ladder safety system.
• The final OSHA deadline for all qualifying fixed ladders is November 18, 2036.
• Stairways with four or more risers or rising more than 30 inches require stair rail systems or handrails.
lessons.low-slope-roofs:
**Low-Slope Roofs and Work Near Roof Edges**

OSHA 1910.28 sets tiered protection requirements for work on low-slope roofs based on proximity to the roof edge. When work is less than 6 feet from the roof edge, stronger protection is required. For work between 6 and less than 15 feet from the edge, specific controls apply. For work 15 feet or more from the roof edge, OSHA allows a designated area combined with enforcement of a work rule prohibiting employees from going within 15 feet of the roof edge without required protection. Distance from the edge determines the required control level — a few steps toward the edge can move an employee from a controlled zone into a fall hazard zone that requires stronger protection.

• Low-slope roof protection requirements under OSHA 1910.28 are tiered by distance from the edge.
• Work less than 6 feet from the roof edge requires stronger fall protection than work farther away.
• For work 15 feet or more from the edge, a designated area plus a work rule prohibiting edge approach may be used.
• Distance from the edge determines the required control — every step closer increases the protection requirement.
lessons.falling-object-protection:
**Falling Object Protection**

When employees are exposed to falling objects from elevated work areas, OSHA 1910.28(c) requires head protection meeting Subpart I criteria and additional controls. Acceptable falling object controls include toeboards, mesh screens, guardrail systems used as barriers, canopy structures, barricades that restrict employee access below elevated work, and keeping materials stored far enough from edges, holes, and openings that they cannot fall. Tools and materials at elevation must be secured, and workers below elevated tasks must wear required hard hats. The best strategy is to prevent objects from falling in the first place and to keep employees out of drop zones through access control and physical barriers.

• Head protection meeting OSHA Subpart I is required when employees are exposed to falling objects.
• Acceptable falling object controls include toeboards, screens, canopies, barricades, and access restrictions.
• Materials near edges, holes, and openings must be stored or secured to prevent displacement.
• The primary strategy is to prevent objects from falling and to keep workers out of drop zones.
